An orison is simply a prayer — a heartfelt, often spoken appeal directed to God or a divine being.

Not every kind of communication with God carries the same feeling. "Orison" specifically suggests a prayer that is:

  • Earnest and humble — the person praying is in a posture of reverence, not bargaining or demanding
  • Spoken or voiced — historically, orisons were uttered aloud, though the word can also apply to silent, deeply felt prayers
  • Devoted — there is a sense of genuine spiritual sincerity behind an orison, not just routine recitation

So while "prayer" is a broad, everyday word, "orison" carries a weight of deep personal devotion. Think of it as a prayer offered from the innermost part of a person's soul.
Register: When is this word used?

This is crucial to understand, because you will almost never hear "orison" in everyday conversation today. It is considered archaic — meaning it was once common but has fallen out of ordinary use. You will encounter it mainly in:

  • Classic literature and poetry (especially works from the 16th to 19th century)
  • Religious texts and hymns of older periods
  • Modern writing that deliberately wants to evoke an old, solemn, or elevated tone

When a modern writer uses "orison" instead of "prayer," they are making a conscious stylistic choice — signaling to the reader that the moment is weighty, sacred, or deeply moving.

• Singular — "an orison": Refers to one specific prayer or act of praying.
    • "She whispered an orison before the battle began."
  • Plural — "orisons": Can refer to a collection of prayers, a prayer session, or a series of devotional acts.
    • "He knelt at dawn to say his orisons, as he had done every morning for thirty years."

The plural form is actually more commonly seen in literature than the singular.

Here are some sentences to help you feel the word in context:

  1. "In the silence of the empty chapel, the monk offered his orison to the heavens."
  2. "Her lips moved in quiet orison as she sat beside her ailing mother."
  3. "The priests' orisons rang through the stone halls of the ancient cathedral."
  4. "Before setting sail into the storm, the captain bowed his head in a final orison."

Notice the consistent mood: solemnity, sincerity, and a certain timeless quality.
The most famous use of this word

You are likely to encounter "orison" most famously in Shakespeare's Hamlet. When Hamlet speaks to Ophelia and tells her to go to a nunnery, he says something along the lines of: go and pray, and remember his sins in those prayers. The word Shakespeare uses for "prayers" there is orisons. This line has made the word famous in English literature, and it is one reason "orison" still lives on in educated vocabulary even though it has otherwise faded from everyday speech.

WordTone/Use
PrayerEveryday, neutral, modern
OrisonArchaic, poetic, deeply devotional
SupplicationBegging or pleading, more desperate in tone
InvocationCalling upon a divine being, often at the start of something formal

Among these, "orison" is the most emotionally intimate and old-world in feel.
The single most important thing to remember

If you ever see the word "orison" or "orisons" — in a poem, a novel, or a religious text — simply understand it as a prayer, spoken with deep sincerity and reverence, in a context that is intentionally solemn or old-fashioned in tone.
